newsitem.title: UK: BA denies Labour deal on windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: BA denies Labour deal on windfall tax.

text.p: British Airways Plc said on Wednesday it had not held any discussions with Britain's Labour Party over a proposed windfall tax on certain companies.

The airline's statement came after Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine on Tuesday repeated newspaper reports that if Labour won the next election it would exempt BA from the proposed tax as a favour to the firm's chief executive, Robert Ayling.
But Ayling said BA had not struck any deals with Labour or any other political parties in relation to the proposed tax.
"I have not sought, nor have I received, any assurances from the leaders of the Labour Party about the windfall tax. I have not discussed the issue with them," he said in a statement.
Labour confirmed at the weekend that Ayling was one of several leading businessmen who dined periodically with party leader Tony Blair and offered him advice in a personal capacity.
Speaking at a business conference, Heseltine said Labour had a clear political commitment to levy a windfall tax.
"We read that British Airways have escaped the net. I've heard that there is no such thing as a free lunch. Evidently, if you work at it, there can be free dinners," he said.

Quizzed by reporters later, Heseltine denied he was accusing BA of striking a sweetheart deal with Labour, which is favoured to beat the ruling Conservative Party in the next election, due by May. Heseltine said he was merely pointing out inconsistencies of the proposed tax by repeating newspaper reports that BA had been excluded.
But a Labour spokesman said the windfall tax would apply to the excess profits of privatised utilities operating in monopoly markets. "BA's not a utility," the spokesman said.
Heseltine's remarks about BA coincided with his accusations that certain British businessmen were a front for Labour.
The statements dismayed many Conservative members of parliament, but Heseltine defied the criticism and dismissed suggestions that he was in a hole and should stop digging.
"You may think we should stop digging. I think we should dig and dig deeper," he told reporters on Wednesday.
